chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said narrated it from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

"Zihar (verbal divorce) does not take effect except upon consummation (or sexual intercourse); so if he has consummated, he is not permitted to have intercourse with her until he expiates. If he was ignorant and did have intercourse, then upon him is one expiation."
And Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Ali ibn Ahmad, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, who said: I said to him:

"Some of your freed slaves claim that if a man speaks the words of Zihar, the expiation becomes obligatory upon him whether he has consummated or not, and they say his 'consummation' is his speaking the words of Zihar, and the expiation was made as a punishment for his speech. And some of them claim that the expiation does not become obligatory until he consummates in the thing he swore upon. If he consummates, the expiation becomes obligatory upon him, and otherwise, there is no expiation upon him." So he (peace be upon him) wrote: "The expiation does not become obligatory until the consummation becomes obligatory."

It was said to him: The intended meaning of 'consummation' (Hinth) in these two hadiths is not the breaking of the oath, but rather its meaning is: if the Zihar is conditional (suspended upon a condition), then when the condition occurs, the expiation becomes obligatory, and if it does not occur, there is no expiation upon him.

And that which indicates this is what Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Abdullah ibn Abi Najran, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: "Zihar is of two types: one is that he says 'You are to me like the back of my mother' and then remains silent; that is the one for which he expiates before having intercourse. If he says 'You are to me like the back of my mother if I do such and such', and he does it and consummates, then upon him is the expiation at the time of consummation."

key_terms.الظِّهَار: Zihar: A form of divorce in Islamic jurisprudence where a husband says to his wife 'You are to me like the back of my mother', making intercourse forbidden until expiation is made.
key_terms.الْحِنْث: Consummation or fulfillment: In this context, it refers to sexual intercourse or the fulfillment of a condition, triggering the obligation of expiation.
key_terms.الْكَفَّارَةُ: Expiation: The penance required to lift the prohibition of Zihar, typically involving freeing a slave, fasting, or feeding the poor.
key_terms.مُعَلَّقاً بِشَرْطٍ: Conditional: Refers to a Zihar statement that is suspended upon the occurrence of a specific event or action.
key_terms.يُوَاقِعَهَا: To have intercourse with her: Refers to the act of sexual consummation with the wife.

ai.seo_question: When does the expiation for Zihar become obligatory: upon speaking the words or upon sexual intercourse?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudential debate regarding whether the expiation (*Kaffarah*) for *Zihar* is triggered by the utterance itself or by the subsequent consummation (*Hinth*) of the marriage. It distinguishes between unconditional declarations, which require expiation before intercourse, and conditional ones, where the penalty applies only if the condition is fulfilled and the couple engages in intimacy. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the actualization of the legal consequence rather than mere verbal intent.
